question: How biased are large language models when they are used as judges to evaluate other models?
criteria: studies large language models used as judges or evaluators
measures or analyzes a bias, reliability problem, or agreement with humans

on_topic.title: Position Bias in Pairwise LLM Evaluation
on_topic.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as judges that compare the outputs of other models. We study position bias in pairwise evaluation across six judge models and 4,000 comparisons. Judges prefer the answer presented first in 62% of the cases where human annotators show no preference. Swapping the order of the answers and averaging the two verdicts reduces the preference to 51%.
passages: We evaluate six judge models on 4,000 pairwise comparisons drawn from three benchmarks. Judges prefer the answer presented first in 62% of the cases where human annotators show no preference. The effect is strongest when the two answers are of similar quality. Swapping the order of the answers and averaging the two verdicts reduces the preference to 51%.

on_topic.title: Self-Preference in LLM Judges
on_topic.abstract: We examine whether language models acting as judges favour outputs produced by their own model family. Across three judge families, judges rate their own family's outputs higher than human raters do. GPT-4 judges favour GPT-4 outputs by 10 percentage points relative to human ratings, and the size of the bias correlates with the perplexity of the evaluated text.
passages: Across three judge families, judges rate outputs from their own family higher than human raters do. GPT-4 judges favour GPT-4 outputs by 10 percentage points relative to human ratings. The size of this self-preference correlates with the perplexity of the evaluated text: judges prefer text they find more predictable.

on_topic.title: Verbosity Bias in Automatic Evaluation
on_topic.abstract: We show that LLM judges reward longer answers regardless of their quality. Increasing answer length by 30% raises scores by 0.4 points on a 10-point scale without any change in correctness. A length-controlled scoring rubric removes most of this effect.
passages: Increasing answer length by 30% raises judge scores by 0.4 points on a 10-point scale without any change in correctness. The bias appears in all five judges we test. A length-controlled scoring rubric removes most of this effect, lowering the gap to 0.1 points.

on_topic.title: How Often Do LLM Judges Agree with Human Raters?
on_topic.abstract: We measure agreement between LLM judges and expert human raters on 2,500 items. Strong judges agree with experts 81% of the time, comparable to the 79% agreement between pairs of experts. Agreement drops to 58% on multi-step reasoning tasks, where judges often accept fluent but wrong solutions.
passages: Strong judges agree with expert raters 81% of the time, comparable to the 79% agreement between pairs of experts. Agreement drops to 58% on multi-step reasoning tasks. On these tasks judges often accept fluent but wrong solutions.

off_topic.title: Crop Disease Detection from Drone Imagery with Lightweight CNNs
off_topic.abstract: We present a lightweight convolutional network for detecting crop diseases in drone imagery. On a new dataset of 12,000 annotated field images, the model reaches 94% accuracy while running at 30 frames per second on an embedded board.

off_topic.title: Solid-State Electrolytes for Fast-Charging Lithium Batteries
off_topic.abstract: We report a sulfide-based solid-state electrolyte that supports fast charging of lithium metal batteries. Cells retain 90% of their capacity after 800 cycles at a 3C charging rate.

off_topic.title: A Faster Exact Algorithm for Graph Coloring on Sparse Graphs
off_topic.abstract: We give an exact algorithm for graph coloring that runs in time exponential only in the degeneracy of the graph. On sparse benchmark graphs it is up to 40 times faster than the best previous exact solver.
